tribe: Ephraim (by residence); Levite by the Chronicler's genealogy

events.title: Yearly pilgrimage to Shiloh
events.summary: Every year he goes up from Ramah to worship and sacrifice at Shiloh, and he gives Hannah a double portion because he loves her.

events.title: Comforts Hannah
events.summary: When Hannah weeps over her childlessness he asks, 'Am I not better to you than ten sons?' The question is tender but misses the depth of her grief.

events.title: Agrees to Hannah's vow
events.summary: He lets Hannah keep Samuel at home until he is weaned and supports her vow to give the boy to the LORD's service.

events.title: Blessed with more children
events.summary: Eli blesses Elkanah and Hannah, and Hannah later bears three more sons and two daughters.

summary: Elkanah was a devout man from Ramathaim-zophim in the hill country of Ephraim and the husband of Hannah and Peninnah. He went up to Shiloh every year to worship, loved Hannah openly even though she had no children, and backed her vow to dedicate their son Samuel to the LORD. He is a quiet, faithful figure in a dark period when Eli's sons were corrupting the sanctuary. The text calls him an Ephraimite, but 1 Chronicles lists him in a Levite family line; both can be true if 'Ephraimite' describes where he lived rather than his tribe.
textSays: Son of Jeroham, from Ramathaim-zophim in Ephraim, with two wives, Hannah and Peninnah (1 Sam 1:1-2). Worshipped yearly at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3). Loved Hannah and gave her a double portion (1 Sam 1:5). Supported her vow (1 Sam 1:23). Listed among the Levites, descendants of Kohath (1 Chr 6:27).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic tradition remembers him as a man who encouraged others to make the pilgrimage to Shiloh, taking a different route each year so more people would join. This is legend, not text.

Many scholars see the Levite genealogy in Chronicles as a later way of explaining why Samuel, a non-priest, could serve at the sanctuary; others take it as historical and read 'Ephraimite' as a geographical label (debated).

voice: Gentle, steady and a little puzzled by his wife's sorrow; speaks plainly and kindly, as a man trying to make things right at home.

events.title: Provokes Hannah
events.summary: Year after year at Shiloh she taunts Hannah for being childless until Hannah weeps and will not eat.

summary: Peninnah was Elkanah's second wife, who had children while Hannah had none. The text calls her Hannah's 'rival' and says she provoked her bitterly every year at the festival. Her story echoes the earlier tension between Sarah and Hagar and between Rachel and Leah.
textSays: Had children while Hannah had none (1 Sam 1:2). Called Hannah's rival, she provoked her to irritate her, year after year (1 Sam 1:6-7).

interpretations.view: Some rabbis claim she taunted Hannah to push her to pray harder; this softens her character but has no basis in the text.

voice: Sharp-tongued and proud of her children; speaks with barbs dressed up as remarks.

alternatives.label: Earlier chronology of the judges period

events.title: Abuses the sacrifices
events.summary: With his brother he takes the best meat by force before the fat is offered to God and sleeps with women serving at the tent entrance. He ignores his father's warning.

events.title: Dies when the ark is captured
events.summary: He carries the ark into battle against the Philistines as if it were a lucky charm. Israel is routed, the ark is taken, and Hophni and Phinehas are killed on the same day, as foretold.

summary: Hophni was the elder son of the priest Eli. The text calls him and his brother 'worthless men' who 'did not know the LORD', because they stole from the sacrifices and abused their office. Both died on one day in battle against the Philistines, the sign a man of God had given Eli.
textSays: Priest at Shiloh with his brother (1 Sam 1:3). Took meat by force and treated the LORD's offering with contempt (1 Sam 2:12-17). Refused to listen to Eli (1 Sam 2:25). His death with his brother foretold (1 Sam 2:34) and fulfilled at Ebenezer/Aphek (1 Sam 4:11).
voice: Entitled and dismissive; talks about holy things as if they were perks of the job.

alternatives.label: Earlier chronology of the judges period

events.title: Corrupts the priesthood
events.summary: Together with Hophni he seizes sacrificial meat and sins with the women who served at the sanctuary.

events.title: Killed in battle; son born
events.summary: He dies when the ark is captured. On hearing the news his pregnant wife goes into labour, names the boy Ichabod, and dies.

summary: Phinehas was Eli's younger son and a priest at Shiloh. He shares his name with the zealous grandson of Aaron, which makes his corruption all the sharper by contrast. He died with his brother when the Philistines took the ark, and his widow named their newborn son Ichabod, 'the glory has departed'.
textSays: Eli's son, priest at Shiloh (1 Sam 1:3); one of the 'worthless men' who despised the LORD's offering (1 Sam 2:12-17). Killed with Hophni (1 Sam 4:11). Father of Ichabod (1 Sam 4:19-21) and of Ahitub (1 Sam 14:3).
voice: Careless and grasping; treats warnings as an old man's fussing.

names.meaning: Where is the glory? / No glory

alternatives.label: Earlier chronology of the judges period

events.title: Named in grief
events.summary: His mother, dying in childbirth after hearing that the ark is taken and her husband and father-in-law are dead, names him Ichabod: 'The glory has departed from Israel.'

summary: Ichabod was the son of Phinehas and grandson of Eli, born on the day the ark of God was captured. His name is a lament, meaning roughly 'no glory', because his mother felt God's presence had left Israel. He is mentioned once more as the uncle of a priest who served with Saul.
textSays: Born as his mother died; named because 'the glory has departed from Israel, for the ark of God has been captured' (1 Sam 4:21-22). His brother Ahitub's son Ahijah served as priest under Saul (1 Sam 14:3).
voice: A name more than a speaker; if he spoke, it would be with the weight of a family that lost everything in one day.

events.title: Sends Saul after lost donkeys
events.summary: When his donkeys stray, Kish sends Saul and a servant to find them. The errand leads Saul to Samuel, who anoints him king.

summary: Kish was a wealthy Benjaminite and the father of Saul, Israel's first king. His lost donkeys set off the chain of events that brought Saul to Samuel. Saul's bones were eventually buried in Kish's family tomb at Zela.
textSays: A Benjaminite, 'a man of standing', son of Abiel (1 Sam 9:1). Father of Saul (1 Sam 9:2). Saul and Jonathan buried in his tomb (2 Sam 21:14). Paul names him as Saul's father (Acts 13:21). Genealogies differ on whether Kish's father was Abiel or Ner (1 Chr 8:33), which affects whether Abner was Saul's uncle or cousin.
voice: Practical and well-off; concerned about his animals and then about his missing son.

alternatives.label: Higher chronology for David's Hebron reign

events.title: Brings David to Saul
events.summary: After David kills Goliath, Abner brings him, still holding the giant's head, before Saul.

events.title: Rebuked by David at the camp
events.summary: David slips into Saul's camp and takes his spear and water jug, then mocks Abner for failing to guard the king.

events.title: Makes Ishbosheth king
events.summary: After Saul's death he sets up Saul's son Ishbosheth as king over Israel at Mahanaim, opposing David.

events.title: Battle at Gibeon; kills Asahel
events.summary: His men lose to Joab's at the pool of Gibeon. Fleeing, he kills Joab's brother Asahel, who would not stop chasing him.

events.title: Defects to David and is murdered
events.summary: After quarrelling with Ishbosheth over Saul's concubine Rizpah, he agrees to bring all Israel to David. Joab kills him at Hebron in revenge. David mourns publicly and curses Joab's act.

summary: Abner was Saul's relative and the commander of his army, the most powerful man in Israel after the king. When Saul died he kept the house of Saul alive by making Ishbosheth king, and fought a long war against David. When Ishbosheth accused him over Saul's concubine Rizpah, Abner switched sides and began bringing the northern tribes to David, but Joab murdered him to avenge his brother Asahel. David's public grief, 'a prince and a great man has fallen this day', helped show Israel he had no part in the killing.
textSays: Son of Ner, Saul's uncle, and commander of the army (1 Sam 14:50-51). Made Ishbosheth king (2 Sam 2:8-9). Killed Asahel (2 Sam 2:23). Went over to David after the Rizpah quarrel (2 Sam 3:7-21). Killed by Joab at the gate of Hebron (2 Sam 3:27). David wept at his grave (2 Sam 3:31-39).

interpretations.view: Many readers see Abner as a realist who served whoever held power, while the narrator uses his death to clear David of blame for the fall of Saul's house.

strengths: Loyal to Saul's family for years
Saw that David's rise was God's will (2 Sam 3:9-10)
failures: Used Saul's concubine in a bid for power (2 Sam 3:7)
turningPoints: Ishbosheth's accusation pushes him to David (2 Sam 3:8-12)

voice: Gruff, proud and blunt, a soldier who knows his worth and says so; quick to anger, quick to strike a deal.

roles: king of Israel (northern tribes) after Saul

events.title: Made king by Abner
events.summary: At forty he is made king over Gilead and the northern tribes and reigns two years, while Judah follows David.

events.title: Accuses Abner
events.summary: He accuses Abner of sleeping with Saul's concubine Rizpah. Abner explodes and vows to give the kingdom to David; Ishbosheth is too afraid to answer.

events.title: Returns Michal to David
events.summary: At David's demand he takes Michal from her husband Paltiel and sends her back to David.

events.title: Murdered in his bed
events.summary: Two of his captains kill him during his midday rest and bring his head to David, who executes them for murdering an innocent man.

summary: Ish-bosheth was a son of Saul whom Abner made king over the northern tribes after Saul died. He was a weak ruler who depended entirely on Abner. Once Abner defected, his support collapsed, and two of his own officers murdered him in his bed. His original name was probably Eshbaal, 'man of Baal' (where 'baal' may simply mean 'lord'); later scribes seem to have replaced 'baal' with 'bosheth', meaning 'shame'.
textSays: Son of Saul, aged forty when he began to reign, reigned two years over Israel (2 Sam 2:8-10). Lost heart when Abner died (2 Sam 4:1). Killed by Rechab and Baanah (2 Sam 4:5-7). Called Eshbaal in Chronicles (1 Chr 8:33).

interpretations.view: Most scholars think 'bosheth' (shame) was substituted for 'baal' by scribes who disliked the Baal element; 'baal' may originally have been a title for the LORD (scholarly-consensus on the substitution, debated on the original meaning).
His two-year reign versus David's seven and a half years in Hebron (2 Sam 2:10-11) suggests either a delay before he was crowned or a gap after his death (debated).

voice: Nervous and hesitant; a reluctant king who speaks as if looking over his shoulder for Abner.

names.meaning: From the mouth of shame (likely a scribal change)

events.title: Lamed as a child
events.summary: He is five when news comes that Saul and Jonathan are dead. His nurse flees with him, he falls, and he is lame in both feet for life.

events.title: Shown kindness by David
events.summary: For Jonathan's sake David restores Saul's land to him and gives him a permanent place at the king's table. He calls himself a 'dead dog' in reply.

events.title: Accused by Ziba
events.summary: During Absalom's revolt his servant Ziba tells David that Mephibosheth stayed in Jerusalem hoping to regain Saul's kingdom. David gives Ziba his property.

events.title: Meets David returning
events.summary: Unwashed and unshaven since David left, he says Ziba deceived him. David splits the land between them; Mephibosheth says Ziba may have it all now that the king is safe.

events.title: Spared
events.summary: When Saul's descendants are handed to the Gibeonites, David spares him because of his oath to Jonathan.

summary: Mephibosheth was Jonathan's son, lame in both feet after a fall in childhood. David brought him to Jerusalem, restored Saul's lands to him and gave him a seat at the royal table, keeping his covenant of friendship with Jonathan. During Absalom's revolt his servant Ziba accused him of disloyalty, and the text leaves it to the reader to decide who was telling the truth. He became a favourite Christian picture of grace shown to the undeserving.
textSays: Lame from age five (2 Sam 4:4). Received Saul's land and ate at David's table 'like one of the king's sons' (2 Sam 9:7-13). Had a young son, Mica (2 Sam 9:12). Accused by Ziba (2 Sam 16:3), defended himself (2 Sam 19:26-28). Spared because of the oath to Jonathan (2 Sam 21:7). Called Merib-baal in Chronicles (1 Chr 8:34). Not the same as Rizpah's son Mephibosheth (2 Sam 21:8).

interpretations.view: Often used as an illustration of grace: a crippled enemy's heir welcomed to the king's table for another's sake.
Readers disagree over whether Ziba lied or Mephibosheth was hedging; David's split decision suggests he was not sure either (debated).

voice: Humble to the point of self-abasement, grateful, with a quiet dignity when wronged.

events.title: Steward for Mephibosheth
events.summary: David puts him, with his fifteen sons and twenty servants, in charge of farming Saul's land for Mephibosheth.

events.title: Brings supplies and an accusation
events.summary: He meets the fleeing David with donkeys and food and claims Mephibosheth hopes to regain the throne. David gives Ziba all Mephibosheth's property.

summary: Ziba was a servant of Saul's household whom David made steward of Mephibosheth's estate. During Absalom's revolt he helped David with supplies but accused his master of treachery, winning Mephibosheth's land. When David returned, he split the property between them, unsure whom to believe.
textSays: Servant of Saul's house with fifteen sons and twenty servants (2 Sam 9:2-10). Brought provisions and accused Mephibosheth (2 Sam 16:1-4). Mephibosheth said Ziba had slandered him (2 Sam 19:26-27). David divided the land (2 Sam 19:29).
voice: Smooth, eager to please the powerful, always ready with a gift and a story.

events.title: Promised to David, given to another
events.summary: Saul offers her to David if he fights the Philistines, hoping they will kill him, but then gives her to Adriel the Meholathite instead.

summary: Merab was Saul's elder daughter. Saul promised her to David as a reward and a trap, then married her to Adriel instead. Many manuscripts and translations name her as the mother of the five grandsons of Saul later handed over to the Gibeonites, although the traditional Hebrew text there reads 'Michal'.
textSays: Saul's elder daughter (1 Sam 14:49). Promised to David, given to Adriel (1 Sam 18:17-19). The five sons whom Michal (or Merab) bore to Adriel were executed by the Gibeonites (2 Sam 21:8-9).

interpretations.view: Most modern versions read 'Merab' in 2 Sam 21:8 with some Hebrew and Greek manuscripts, since Adriel was Merab's husband; the KJV keeps 'Michal' and Jewish tradition explains that Michal raised Merab's sons (debated).

voice: Reserved; a royal daughter used as a political piece, speaking little of her own wishes.

events.title: Cause of Abner's break
events.summary: Ishbosheth accuses Abner of sleeping with her, which in that culture was a claim to the dead king's throne.

events.title: Guards her sons' bodies
events.summary: After her two sons and five of Saul's grandsons are executed by the Gibeonites, she spreads sackcloth on a rock and keeps birds and wild animals off the bodies from harvest until the rains. Moved by her vigil, David gives Saul's family an honourable burial.

summary: Rizpah, daughter of Aiah, was a concubine of Saul and mother of his sons Armoni and Mephibosheth (not Jonathan's son). After her sons were executed to end a famine, she kept watch over their bodies for months. Her silent protest moved David to bury Saul and Jonathan's bones properly, and only then 'God responded to the plea for the land'.
textSays: Daughter of Aiah, Saul's concubine (2 Sam 3:7). Mother of Armoni and Mephibosheth (2 Sam 21:8). Kept vigil over the bodies (2 Sam 21:10). David then buried the bones of Saul and Jonathan (2 Sam 21:11-14).
voice: Few words; fierce, patient grief that speaks by staying.

events.title: Captured at Ziklag and rescued
events.summary: Amalekite raiders carry her and Abigail off from Ziklag; David pursues and rescues them.

events.title: Mother of David's firstborn
events.summary: At Hebron she bears Amnon, David's eldest son.

summary: Ahinoam from Jezreel (a town in Judah, not the northern city) was one of David's earliest wives, married while he was an outlaw. She went with him to Gath and Ziklag and became the mother of Amnon, his firstborn. She should not be confused with Saul's wife Ahinoam, daughter of Ahimaaz, though a few scholars suggest they were the same woman.
textSays: David married Ahinoam of Jezreel (1 Sam 25:43). With David at Gath and Ziklag (1 Sam 27:3); taken captive and rescued (1 Sam 30:5). Mother of Amnon (2 Sam 3:2). Saul's wife was also named Ahinoam (1 Sam 14:50).

interpretations.view: A minority view (associated with Jon Levenson) proposes that David took Saul's wife Ahinoam, which would explain Nathan's words that God gave David 'your master's wives' (2 Sam 12:8). Most scholars treat them as two different women (speculative).

voice: Quiet and enduring, a woman who shared David's years on the run.

names.meaning: Oppression, or perhaps a place name

events.title: Bears Absalom at Hebron
events.summary: She bears Absalom, David's third son, during his reign at Hebron.

summary: Maacah was the daughter of Talmai, king of Geshur, a small Aramean kingdom east of the Sea of Galilee, and was probably married to David as part of an alliance. She was the mother of Absalom and almost certainly of Tamar, his full sister. Absalom fled to his grandfather in Geshur after killing Amnon. Several other women in Kings and Chronicles share her name, including Rehoboam's wife and Asa's queen mother.
textSays: Daughter of Talmai king of Geshur, mother of Absalom (2 Sam 3:3). Absalom fled to Talmai (2 Sam 13:37-38). Tamar is called Absalom's sister (2 Sam 13:1); that Maacah was her mother is inferred, not stated.
voice: Dignified and foreign-born, a king's daughter in a rival king's court.

events.title: Obsessed with Tamar
events.summary: He makes himself ill with desire for his half-sister Tamar; his cousin Jonadab suggests he pretend to be sick and ask for her.

events.title: Rapes Tamar
events.summary: When Tamar brings food he seizes her. She pleads with him not to do this 'outrageous thing', but he overpowers her.

events.title: Throws her out
events.summary: His desire turns to hatred and he has her thrown out and the door bolted.

events.title: Killed by Absalom
events.summary: Two years later Absalom invites him to a sheep-shearing feast and has his servants kill him.

summary: Amnon was David's firstborn son and heir. He raped his half-sister Tamar and then cast her out in disgust. David was angry but did nothing, and two years later Tamar's brother Absalom had Amnon murdered. The story is the first fulfilment of Nathan's warning that 'the sword shall never depart' from David's house after his sin with Bathsheba.
textSays: Firstborn of David by Ahinoam (2 Sam 3:2). Raped Tamar, then hated her more than he had loved her (2 Sam 13:14-15). David was very angry (2 Sam 13:21) but the Greek text adds that he would not punish Amnon because he loved him as firstborn. Killed by Absalom's men (2 Sam 13:28-29).

interpretations.view: The Mishnah (Avot 5:16) contrasts Amnon's love, which depended on something and so ended, with the selfless love of David and Jonathan.
Read as a case study of lust as consumption, of a father's failure to act, and of how sin in David's house repeats his own abuse of power.

voice: Self-pitying, impulsive and entitled; speaks of what he wants, not of the other person.

events.title: Sent to Amnon's house
events.summary: At David's order she goes to bake bread for her 'sick' half-brother Amnon.

events.title: Resists and is raped
events.summary: She refuses, calls the act a disgrace in Israel and suggests he ask the king for her properly, but he forces her.

events.title: Mourns publicly
events.summary: Thrown out, she tears her royal robe, puts ashes on her head and goes away crying. She lives 'desolate' in Absalom's house.

summary: Tamar was David's daughter and Absalom's full sister. Her half-brother Amnon tricked her into his room and raped her, ignoring her clear and courageous protest. She tore her princess's robe and cried aloud rather than stay silent, then lived on in her brother's house as a 'desolate woman'. Absalom named his own daughter after her.
textSays: Beautiful sister of Absalom (2 Sam 13:1). Argued against the assault (2 Sam 13:12-13). Tore her long-sleeved robe and mourned (2 Sam 13:18-19). Remained desolate in Absalom's house (2 Sam 13:20). Absalom's daughter was named Tamar (2 Sam 14:27). Listed as David's daughter (1 Chr 3:9).

interpretations.view: Tamar is read as a model of a victim's clear voice and as an indictment of a family and court that silenced her ('keep quiet', 2 Sam 13:20).
Often treated mainly as a step in the story of Absalom and as a warning about lust; her own voice received less attention.

voice: Clear, reasoned and brave; she argues from the law and from honour, and then from grief.

events.title: Declares himself king
events.summary: As David lies dying, he gathers chariots and runners and holds a feast at En-rogel with Joab and Abiathar, leaving out Nathan, Zadok, Benaiah and Solomon.

events.title: Plan collapses
events.summary: Hearing that Solomon has been anointed, his guests scatter. He clings to the horns of the altar until Solomon promises to spare him if he behaves.

events.title: Asks for Abishag; executed
events.summary: Through Bathsheba he asks to marry Abishag, David's last companion. Solomon reads it as a claim to the throne and has Benaiah kill him.

summary: Adonijah, son of David and Haggith, was the eldest surviving son after Amnon and Absalom died, and expected to be king. David had 'never crossed him', and he tried to take the throne while his father was dying, backed by Joab and the priest Abiathar. Nathan and Bathsheba moved David to crown Solomon instead. Adonijah was spared, but after he asked to marry Abishag, Solomon saw a renewed claim to the throne and had him executed.
textSays: Son of Haggith, born at Hebron (2 Sam 3:4). Handsome, born after Absalom; David never rebuked him (1 Kgs 1:6). Exalted himself as king (1 Kgs 1:5). Took hold of the altar (1 Kgs 1:50). Admitted the kingdom had become Solomon's 'from the LORD' (1 Kgs 2:15). Killed by Benaiah (1 Kgs 2:25).
voice: Confident and charming, used to getting his way; speaks like the heir he thinks he is.

roles: ancestor of Jesus in Luke's genealogy

events.title: Named in Luke's genealogy
events.summary: Luke traces Jesus' ancestry back through Nathan rather than Solomon.

summary: Nathan was a son of David born in Jerusalem, and one of four sons of Bathsheba (called Bath-shua in Chronicles). He is not the prophet Nathan. His importance is that Luke's genealogy of Jesus runs through him, while Matthew's runs through Solomon.
textSays: Born in Jerusalem to David and Bathshua (1 Chr 3:5; 2 Sam 5:14). His house mourns in Zechariah's vision (Zech 12:12). In Jesus' genealogy (Luke 3:31).

interpretations.view: Some explain the two genealogies by saying Luke gives Mary's line through Nathan and Matthew gives Joseph's legal line through Solomon (a view going back at least to the Reformation era); others, following Julius Africanus, appeal to levirate marriage (debated).
Many scholars think the two genealogies reflect separate traditions with different theological aims, and that tracing through Nathan avoided the cursed line of Jehoiachin (Jer 22:30) (debated).

voice: Unknown; a quiet royal son remembered mainly for his descendants.

events.title: Curses the fleeing David
events.summary: At Bahurim he throws stones and dust at David, calling him a man of blood who stole Saul's throne. David stops Abishai from killing him: 'the LORD has told him' to curse.

events.title: Begs forgiveness
events.summary: When David returns, Shimei hurries to meet him with a thousand Benjaminites and confesses. David swears not to kill him.

events.title: Confined and executed by Solomon
events.summary: On David's deathbed advice, Solomon confines him to Jerusalem. Three years later he goes to Gath after runaway slaves, and Solomon has Benaiah kill him.

summary: Shimei, a relative of Saul, cursed David to his face when David fled from Absalom, blaming him for the fall of Saul's family. David bore it patiently and later pardoned him. But on his deathbed David told Solomon not to let Shimei go unpunished. Solomon restricted him to Jerusalem, and when Shimei broke the terms he was executed.
textSays: Of Saul's clan, son of Gera (2 Sam 16:5). Cursed David as a 'man of blood' (2 Sam 16:7-8). Pardoned under oath (2 Sam 19:23). David's charge to Solomon (1 Kgs 2:8-9). Executed after leaving Jerusalem (1 Kgs 2:46).

interpretations.view: Some readers admire David's restraint and find his deathbed instruction troubling; others see Solomon's action as lawful because Shimei broke a sworn agreement (debated).

voice: Bitter, loud and partisan; later grovelling and eager to be on the winning side.

events.title: Sent back as a spy
events.summary: He meets David on the Mount of Olives with torn clothes and dust on his head. David sends him back to pretend loyalty to Absalom and defeat Ahithophel's advice.

events.title: Joins Absalom
events.summary: He greets Absalom with 'Long live the king!' and explains his switch with careful double meanings.

events.title: Defeats Ahithophel's plan
events.summary: Ahithophel urges an immediate strike on the exhausted David. Hushai paints vivid pictures of David as a bear robbed of her cubs and persuades Absalom to wait and gather all Israel.

events.title: Warns David
events.summary: He passes the plan to the priests Zadok and Abiathar so David can cross the Jordan in time.

summary: Hushai the Archite held the title 'the king's friend' at David's court. When Absalom rebelled, David sent him back to Jerusalem as a double agent. Hushai won Absalom's trust and talked him out of Ahithophel's sound advice to strike at once, giving David time to escape and regroup. The narrator says this happened because 'the LORD had ordained' to defeat Ahithophel's counsel in answer to David's prayer.
textSays: An Archite (2 Sam 15:32), David's friend (2 Sam 15:37; 1 Chr 27:33). Gave advice that seemed better to Absalom, 'for the LORD had ordained to defeat the good counsel of Ahithophel' (2 Sam 17:14). David had prayed that Ahithophel's counsel be turned to foolishness (2 Sam 15:31).
voice: Warm, quick-witted and theatrical; a master of vivid images and loyal double meanings.

names.meaning: Brother of folly (perhaps a deliberate distortion)

skills.name: Strategic counsel, treated 'as if one consulted the word of God'

events.title: Joins Absalom's revolt
events.summary: Absalom summons him from Giloh. When David hears, he prays that the LORD will turn his counsel to foolishness.

events.title: Advises Absalom to take the harem
events.summary: He tells Absalom to sleep with David's concubines publicly to make the break final; it fulfils Nathan's word (2 Sam 12:11-12).

events.title: Advice rejected; suicide
events.summary: He proposes to strike David that night with twelve thousand men. When Hushai's plan is preferred, he goes home, puts his affairs in order and hangs himself.

summary: Ahithophel of Giloh was David's most respected adviser, whose counsel was treated almost like an oracle. He joined Absalom's rebellion, perhaps partly from resentment: he seems to have been Bathsheba's grandfather. His plan to strike David immediately would likely have worked, but Absalom followed Hushai instead, and Ahithophel, seeing the revolt was lost, went home and hanged himself.
textSays: The Gilonite, David's counsellor (2 Sam 15:12). His advice was esteemed like God's word (2 Sam 16:23). Hanged himself (2 Sam 17:23). His son Eliam was one of David's mighty men (2 Sam 23:34); Bathsheba's father was named Eliam (2 Sam 11:3).

interpretations.view: If the two Eliams are the same man, Ahithophel was Bathsheba's grandfather, which would explain his betrayal of David (speculative; the text does not connect them).
Many interpreters see him as a type of Judas: a trusted friend who betrayed the king and then hanged himself (compare Ps 41:9; Matt 27:5).

voice: Cool, precise and coldly practical; speaks in short, confident plans.

events.title: Famous exploits
events.summary: He kills two champions of Moab, goes down into a pit on a snowy day and kills a lion, and kills a giant Egyptian with the man's own spear.

events.title: Over the Cherethites and Pelethites
events.summary: David puts him in charge of the foreign royal guard.

events.title: Backs Solomon
events.summary: With Zadok and Nathan he escorts Solomon on David's mule to be anointed king.

events.title: Carries out Solomon's sentences
events.summary: He executes Adonijah, Joab (at the altar) and Shimei, and replaces Joab as army commander.

summary: Benaiah, son of the priest Jehoiada of Kabzeel, was one of David's bravest warriors, famous for killing a lion in a pit on a snowy day. He commanded David's foreign bodyguard and stayed loyal to David's choice of Solomon. Under Solomon he carried out the executions of Adonijah, Joab and Shimei and became commander of the army. His father is a different Jehoiada from the later high priest who protected Joash.
textSays: Son of Jehoiada of Kabzeel (2 Sam 23:20). Over the Cherethites and Pelethites (2 Sam 8:18). Honoured among the thirty (2 Sam 23:22-23). Supported Solomon (1 Kgs 1:36-37). Put over the army in Joab's place (1 Kgs 2:35). His father is called a chief priest (1 Chr 27:5).
voice: Terse, fearless and obedient; a soldier who answers 'Amen' and acts.

events.title: Priest beside Abiathar
events.summary: He serves as one of David's two chief priests.

events.title: Carries the ark and returns it
events.summary: When David flees Absalom, Zadok brings the ark, but David sends it back: if God favours him, he will bring him back to it.

events.title: Relays Hushai's news
events.summary: Through his son Ahimaaz he passes intelligence to David.

events.title: Anoints Solomon
events.summary: He anoints Solomon with oil from the tabernacle at Gihon, and the people shout 'Long live King Solomon!'

events.title: Sole chief priest
events.summary: Solomon puts him in Abiathar's place.

summary: Zadok was a priest who served David alongside Abiathar and stayed loyal through Absalom's revolt. When Adonijah tried to seize the throne, Zadok sided with Solomon and anointed him king. Solomon then made him sole chief priest, and his descendants, the Zadokites, led the Jerusalem priesthood for centuries. Ezekiel singles them out as the faithful priests, and the later Sadducees probably take their name from him.
textSays: Son of Ahitub, priest with Abiathar (2 Sam 8:17). Brought and returned the ark (2 Sam 15:24-29). Anointed Solomon (1 Kgs 1:39). Replaced Abiathar (1 Kgs 2:35). Descended from Aaron through Eleazar (1 Chr 6:4-8). The sons of Zadok alone may come near to God in Ezekiel's temple (Ezek 44:15).

interpretations.view: Some scholars suggest Zadok was originally a Jebusite priest of Jerusalem whom David absorbed, and that the Aaronic genealogy was added later; others accept the Chronicler's genealogy (debated).
The name of the Sadducees probably comes from Zadok, and the Qumran community called its priests 'sons of Zadok' (scholarly-consensus on the Qumran usage).

voice: Calm, loyal and ceremonious; a priest who trusts God with outcomes.

roles: keeper of the ephod for David
last of Eli's line in high office

events.title: Escapes the massacre at Nob
events.summary: When Saul's man Doeg kills the priests of Nob, Abiathar alone escapes to David, who takes responsibility and protects him.

events.title: Brings the ephod
events.summary: With the ephod, a priestly object used for seeking God's yes-or-no answers, he helps David inquire of the LORD.

events.title: Loyal during Absalom's revolt
events.summary: With Zadok he brings out the ark and then stays in Jerusalem to help David.

events.title: Backs Adonijah and is banished
events.summary: He supports Adonijah's claim. Solomon spares his life because he served David, but sends him home to Anathoth, fulfilling the word against Eli's house.

summary: Abiathar, son of Ahimelech, was the only priest to survive Saul's massacre at Nob. He joined David as a fugitive and served him faithfully for decades, carrying the ephod and later sharing the chief priesthood with Zadok. In old age he backed Adonijah for the throne. Solomon banished him to Anathoth, and the narrator notes that this fulfilled the prophecy against Eli's family. Jesus mentions him in connection with David eating the holy bread.
textSays: Son of Ahimelech, escaped to David (1 Sam 22:20). Brought the ephod (1 Sam 23:6). Priest with Zadok (2 Sam 15:29). Supported Adonijah (1 Kgs 1:7). Banished to Anathoth 'to fulfil the word of the LORD concerning the house of Eli' (1 Kgs 2:26-27). Named by Jesus (Mark 2:26).

interpretations.view: 1 Samuel 21 says Ahimelech was priest when David ate the bread. Some explain Mark's 'in the time of Abiathar' as referring to the section of scripture or the era of the better-known priest; others see a slip by Mark or a copyist (debated).
His banishment is read as the long fulfilment of judgment on Eli's corrupt house (1 Sam 2:30-36). Jeremiah, a priest from Anathoth, may have descended from him (speculative).

voice: Weathered and loyal, a survivor who has seen a king's violence; cautious about the future.

alternatives.label: Lower date from Josephus' Tyrian king list

events.title: Builds David's palace
events.summary: He sends cedar, carpenters and stonemasons to build a house for David.

events.title: Treaty with Solomon for the temple
events.summary: He supplies cedar and cypress from Lebanon in exchange for wheat and oil; the two kings make a treaty.

events.title: Unimpressed by Galilee towns
events.summary: Solomon gives him twenty towns in Galilee. Hiram calls them 'Cabul', meaning roughly 'good for nothing'.

events.title: Joint fleet
events.summary: His sailors crew Solomon's ships from Ezion-geber to Ophir, bringing gold.

summary: Hiram was the king of Tyre, the great Phoenician port, and a friend and trading partner of David and Solomon. He supplied the cedar timber and skilled craftsmen for David's palace and Solomon's temple and shared in Solomon's sea trade. Josephus, using Tyrian records, places his reign in the tenth century BC. He is different from Hiram (Huram-abi) the bronze-worker who cast the temple's pillars.
textSays: Sent materials for David's house (2 Sam 5:11). 'Always loved David' (1 Kgs 5:1). Blessed the LORD for giving David a wise son (1 Kgs 5:7). Treaty with Solomon (1 Kgs 5:12). Received twenty Galilean towns (1 Kgs 9:11-13). Another Hiram, a craftsman from Tyre, made the bronze work (1 Kgs 7:13-14).

interpretations.view: Josephus (*Against Apion* 1.17-18) cites Tyrian annals naming Hiram son of Abibaal; most historians accept a real Hiram I in the tenth century, though exact dates depend on how the Tyrian list is calculated (debated).

voice: Businesslike, generous and diplomatic; a merchant-king who speaks in terms of fair exchange.

events.title: Tears his cloak into twelve pieces
events.summary: Meeting Jeroboam outside Jerusalem, he tears his new cloak into twelve pieces and gives him ten: God will tear ten tribes from Solomon's son because of Solomon's idolatry.

events.title: Foretells the end of Jeroboam's house
events.summary: Old and blind, he recognises Jeroboam's disguised wife and tells her their sick son will die and Jeroboam's dynasty will be wiped out for its idolatry.

summary: Ahijah was a prophet from Shiloh who announced the split of Solomon's kingdom. He dramatically tore his cloak into twelve pieces and gave ten to Jeroboam, promising him the northern tribes and a lasting dynasty if he obeyed God. When Jeroboam turned to golden calves, the now-blind Ahijah told his wife that their son would die and the dynasty would end, which happened under Nadab.
textSays: A prophet from Shiloh (1 Kgs 11:29). Symbolic tearing of the cloak (1 Kgs 11:30-31). Promised Jeroboam a 'sure house' if he obeyed (1 Kgs 11:38). Prophesied against Jeroboam's house (1 Kgs 14:10-11), fulfilled by Baasha (1 Kgs 15:29). Chronicles mentions his written prophecy (2 Chr 9:29).
voice: Solemn and vivid; acts out his message, then speaks hard words without softening them.

events.title: Speech on Mount Zemaraim
events.summary: Before battle he calls on Jeroboam's army not to fight the LORD, the God of their fathers, pointing to David's covenant and Judah's lawful priests.

events.title: Victory over Jeroboam
events.summary: Surrounded by an ambush, Judah cries to the LORD and the priests blow trumpets; Israel is routed and Abijah takes Bethel and other towns.

summary: Abijah (called Abijam in Kings) reigned over Judah for three years, about 913 to 911 BC. Kings gives a negative verdict: he 'walked in all the sins of his father' and his heart was not wholly true to the LORD, yet God kept a lamp burning in Jerusalem for David's sake. Chronicles instead records his speech and victory over Jeroboam, showing a king who at least appealed to the LORD in battle. The text's overall verdict is mixed.
textSays: Reigned three years in Jerusalem; walked in his father's sins (1 Kgs 15:1-3). Kept on the throne for David's sake (1 Kgs 15:4-5). War with Jeroboam (1 Kgs 15:7). His mother was Maacah daughter of Abishalom (1 Kgs 15:2), also called Micaiah daughter of Uriel (2 Chr 13:2). Defeated Jeroboam 'because they relied on the LORD' (2 Chr 13:18). Had fourteen wives (2 Chr 13:21). In Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:7).

interpretations.view: Kings and Chronicles are often read as complementary: a king with a generally poor record who nevertheless relied on the LORD in one crisis.
Many scholars see the speech in Chronicles as the Chronicler's own composition setting out his theology of the Davidic kingship and the Jerusalem priesthood (debated).

voice: Confident and rhetorical, fond of appeals to tradition and legitimacy.

events.title: Accession and early reform
events.summary: He becomes king and does what is right in the LORD's eyes. He drives out the male cult prostitutes, removes his fathers' idols and foreign altars, and commands Judah to seek the LORD.

events.title: Ten years of peace and building
events.summary: The land is quiet, and he uses the peace to build fortified cities with walls, towers and gates, and to raise a large army.

events.title: Victory over Zerah the Cushite
events.summary: A vast army under Zerah the Cushite invades. Asa prays, 'LORD, there is none like you to help, between the mighty and the weak; help us, for we rely on you.' Judah wins at Mareshah and pursues the enemy to Gerar.

events.title: Azariah's challenge and covenant renewal
events.summary: The prophet Azariah son of Oded tells him, 'The LORD is with you while you are with him.' Asa removes idols, repairs the altar and gathers Judah and northern migrants to swear a covenant to seek the LORD with all their heart.

events.title: Deposes the queen mother
events.summary: He removes his grandmother Maacah from her position as queen mother because she made an obscene image for Asherah, and burns the image in the Kidron Valley.

events.title: Baasha fortifies Ramah
events.summary: Baasha of Israel fortifies Ramah, a few miles north of Jerusalem, to cut off traffic to and from Judah.

events.title: Buys an alliance with Ben-hadad
events.summary: Asa sends silver and gold from the temple and palace to Ben-hadad of Damascus, who breaks his treaty with Baasha and raids northern Israel. Baasha withdraws, and Asa uses his stones to fortify Geba and Mizpah.

events.title: Rebuked by Hanani the seer
events.summary: Hanani tells him he relied on the king of Aram instead of the LORD: 'the eyes of the LORD run to and fro throughout the whole earth' to support those whose hearts are fully his. Asa angrily puts Hanani in the stocks and oppresses some of the people.

events.title: Disease in his feet
events.summary: In his thirty-ninth year he develops a severe disease in his feet, and 'even in his disease he did not seek the LORD, but the physicians'.

events.title: Death and honoured burial
events.summary: He dies in his forty-first year and is buried in a tomb he had cut for himself, laid on a bier of spices, with a very great fire made in his honour.

summary:
Asa was the third king of Judah after the kingdom split, reigning about forty-one years (roughly 911/910 to 870/869 BC on Edwin Thiele's widely used chronology). The verdict of the text is that he 'did what was right in the eyes of the LORD, as David his father had done' and that his heart was 'wholly true to the LORD all his days', though the high places, local hilltop shrines, were not all removed. He is one of only a handful of Judean kings compared favourably with David.

His early reign was a model of reform. He cleared out idols and cult prostitutes, deposed his own grandmother Maacah as queen mother for making an Asherah image, and led a national covenant renewal. When a huge army under Zerah the Cushite invaded, he prayed a short, honest prayer of dependence, and Judah won.

His later years tell a different story. When Baasha of Israel blockaded Judah, Asa emptied the temple treasury to bribe Ben-hadad of Damascus into attacking Israel. It worked politically, but the seer Hanani told him he had relied on a foreign king instead of God. Asa jailed the prophet and oppressed his people, and when his feet became diseased he sought physicians but not the LORD. Chronicles uses his life to show that a strong start does not guarantee a faithful finish.
textSays:
Son of Abijah; reigned forty-one years in Jerusalem (1 Kgs 15:8-10). Did right as David did; removed cult prostitutes and idols; deposed Maacah (1 Kgs 15:11-13). High places not removed, yet his heart was wholly true (1 Kgs 15:14). Bribed Ben-hadad against Baasha (1 Kgs 15:18-20). Diseased in his feet in old age (1 Kgs 15:23).

Chronicles adds ten years of peace (2 Chr 14:1), the victory over Zerah (2 Chr 14:9-15), Azariah's prophecy and the covenant (2 Chr 15:1-15), Hanani's rebuke and Asa's harsh response (2 Chr 16:7-10), and that he sought physicians not the LORD (2 Chr 16:12). He appears in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:7-8).

interpretations.view: Chronicles shapes Asa's life around 'seeking' and 'relying on' the LORD: blessing when he relies on God (2 Chr 14:11; 16:8), trouble when he relies on Aram. Many see this as the Chronicler's teaching on immediate moral consequences.

Kings says the high places were not removed (1 Kgs 15:14), while Chronicles says he removed them (2 Chr 14:3-5) yet also that they were not removed from Israel (2 Chr 15:17). Common harmonisations: he removed pagan shrines but not local shrines to the LORD; or he removed them early but they returned; or 'Israel' in 2 Chr 15:17 means the north. Others see two sources with different emphases (debated).

Some read 2 Chr 16:12 as condemning reliance on doctors instead of God; most commentators say the fault was seeking help without God, not medicine itself, and some suggest the 'physicians' may have used pagan healing practices (debated).
The Talmud (Sotah 10a) connects his foot disease to conscripting scholars and even bridegrooms for labour in 1 Kgs 15:22, reading the punishment as fitting the offence (tradition).

strengths: Bold reform, even against his own grandmother (1 Kgs 15:13)
Humble prayer of dependence in crisis (2 Chr 14:11)
Led the people in wholehearted covenant renewal (2 Chr 15:12-15)
failures: Used temple treasure to buy a foreign alliance (1 Kgs 15:18)
Imprisoned the prophet who rebuked him (2 Chr 16:10)
Oppressed some of the people (2 Chr 16:10)
Did not seek the LORD in illness (2 Chr 16:12)
turningPoints: Azariah's word, 'if you seek him he will be found by you' (2 Chr 15:2)
Baasha's blockade at Ramah and the choice to pay Ben-hadad (2 Chr 16:1-3)

context:
Asa reigned early in the divided kingdom, when Judah and Israel were often at war over their shared border just north of Jerusalem. Aram (Syria), based in Damascus, was emerging as the main power to the north, and both Hebrew kingdoms courted it. Egypt to the south had recently raided Judah under Shishak (1 Kgs 14:25-26), and Zerah's invasion may reflect an Egyptian-backed force from the south (scholarly views differ on who Zerah was).

Asa's long reign overlapped with several northern kings: Jeroboam I, Nadab, Baasha, Elah, Zimri, Omri and the start of Ahab. Chronicles' figures for his thirty-fifth and thirty-sixth years (2 Chr 15:19; 16:1) clash with Kings, where Baasha died in Asa's twenty-sixth year (1 Kgs 16:8). Some scholars, following Thiele, count those years from the division of the kingdom rather than Asa's accession; others suspect a copying error (debated).
legacy: Asa was remembered as one of Judah's good kings, and his son Jehoshaphat continued his reforms (1 Kgs 22:43). His story is a classic biblical warning about finishing well: a man of great early faith who in later years trusted political deals and resented correction. Hanani's line about the eyes of the LORD running through the whole earth (2 Chr 16:9) became a widely quoted promise. Jeremiah later mentions the cistern Asa built at Mizpah (Jer 41:9).
voice: Decisive and earnest in his early years, praying in short plain sentences; later guarded, defensive and quick to take offence at criticism.

events.title: Assassinated at Gibbethon
events.summary: While besieging the Philistine town of Gibbethon he is killed by Baasha, who then wipes out the whole house of Jeroboam, as Ahijah had foretold.

summary: Nadab, son of Jeroboam I, ruled Israel for about two years (around 910 to 909 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil and walked in his father's sin of calf worship. He was murdered by Baasha during a siege, ending Jeroboam's dynasty after only two kings.
textSays: Reigned two years; did evil, walking in Jeroboam's way (1 Kgs 15:25-26). Killed by Baasha at Gibbethon (1 Kgs 15:27-28). His family destroyed according to Ahijah's word (1 Kgs 15:29-30).
voice: Little recorded; imagine a young heir confident in a throne that was already doomed.

events.title: Seizes the throne
events.summary: He kills Nadab and wipes out Jeroboam's family.

events.title: Blockades Judah at Ramah
events.summary: He fortifies Ramah against Asa, but withdraws when Ben-hadad of Damascus, bribed by Asa, attacks northern Israel.

events.title: Condemned by Jehu son of Hanani
events.summary: The prophet tells him that because he followed Jeroboam's sins, his house will be swept away like Jeroboam's.

summary: Baasha, from the tribe of Issachar, killed Nadab and made himself king of Israel, reigning about twenty-four years (around 909 to 886 BC) from Tirzah. The verdict of the text is that he did evil and kept Jeroboam's calf worship. He fought Asa of Judah throughout his reign. The prophet Jehu son of Hanani foretold that his dynasty would fall, and his son Elah was murdered by Zimri after two years.
textSays: Son of Ahijah of Issachar; killed Nadab (1 Kgs 15:27). Reigned twenty-four years at Tirzah and did evil (1 Kgs 15:33-34). War with Asa all their days (1 Kgs 15:16). Fortified Ramah (1 Kgs 15:17). Jehu son of Hanani's oracle (1 Kgs 16:1-4). Zimri destroyed his house (1 Kgs 16:11-13).
voice: Hard, ambitious soldier-king; speaks the language of opportunity and force.

names.meaning: Uncertain; perhaps 'servant of the LORD' or 'my sheaf'

events.title: Proclaimed king by the army
events.summary: When Zimri murders King Elah, the army at Gibbethon makes its commander Omri king. He besieges Tirzah and Zimri burns the palace over himself.

events.title: Civil war with Tibni
events.summary: Half the people follow Tibni; after several years Omri's side wins.

events.title: Founds Samaria
events.summary: He buys the hill of Samaria from Shemer for two talents of silver and builds a new capital, which remains Israel's capital until its fall.

summary: Omri was an army commander who became king of Israel during a civil war and reigned about twelve years (around 885 to 874 BC, including years of rivalry with Tibni). The verdict of the text is that he 'did more evil than all who were before him'. Kings gives him only a few verses, but he was one of Israel's most important rulers politically: he built Samaria as a new capital and founded a dynasty so famous that Assyrian records called Israel 'the house of Omri' long after it ended. The Moabite Mesha Stele says Omri oppressed Moab.
textSays: Commander made king by the army (1 Kgs 16:16). Defeated Zimri and Tibni (1 Kgs 16:17-22). Reigned twelve years, six at Tirzah (1 Kgs 16:23). Bought and built Samaria (1 Kgs 16:24). Did more evil than all before him (1 Kgs 16:25-26). Micah condemns 'the statutes of Omri' (Mic 6:16).

interpretations.view: The Mesha Stele (about 840 BC) and Assyrian inscriptions ('Bit-Humri', house of Omri; Jehu called 'son of Omri' on the Black Obelisk) confirm his importance (scholarly-consensus). Archaeologists also credit the Omrides with major building at Samaria, Megiddo, Hazor and Jezreel, though dating some of it is debated.

voice: Shrewd, practical and ambitious; a general turned statesman who thinks in terms of land, walls and treaties.

events.title: Failed fleet with Jehoshaphat
events.summary: He joins Jehoshaphat in building ships for trade, but they are wrecked; Jehoshaphat later refuses a second venture.

events.title: Falls and consults Baal-zebub
events.summary: Injured in a fall through a lattice in his upper room, he sends to ask Baal-zebub, god of Ekron, whether he will recover. Elijah intercepts the messengers: he will die.

events.title: Sends soldiers against Elijah
events.summary: Two companies sent to arrest Elijah are consumed by fire; the third captain begs for mercy, and Elijah goes to the king and repeats the sentence. Ahaziah dies.

summary: Ahaziah, son of Ahab and Jezebel, reigned over Israel for about two years (around 853 to 852 BC by inclusive counting). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, following his father, his mother and Jeroboam, and served Baal. After a fall he sought a foreign god's oracle instead of the LORD, and Elijah announced his death. He had no son, so his brother Jehoram succeeded him.
textSays: Reigned two years over Israel; did evil and served Baal (1 Kgs 22:51-53). Moab rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 1:1). Fell and consulted Baal-zebub (2 Kgs 1:2). Died according to Elijah's word; no son, Jehoram reigned (2 Kgs 1:17).
voice: Imperious yet fearful; a sick king who sends soldiers to fix what only repentance could.

events.title: Campaign against Mesha of Moab
events.summary: With Jehoshaphat and the king of Edom he marches against Moab. Elisha promises water and victory for Jehoshaphat's sake, but when Mesha sacrifices his son on the wall, the allies withdraw.

events.title: Naaman's letter
events.summary: Receiving a letter asking him to heal Naaman, he tears his clothes, suspecting a trick, until Elisha asks for Naaman to be sent to him.

events.title: Siege of Samaria
events.summary: During a terrible famine under Aramean siege he blames Elisha and seeks his life; Elisha foretells relief the next day, and the Arameans flee in the night.

events.title: Killed by Jehu
events.summary: Wounded fighting Hazael at Ramoth-gilead, he recovers at Jezreel. Jehu shoots him with an arrow on Naboth's land, fulfilling Elijah's word against Ahab.

summary: Jehoram (also spelled Joram), son of Ahab, reigned over Israel for about twelve years (around 852 to 841 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, 'though not like his father and mother', because he removed Baal's sacred pillar, but he kept Jeroboam's sins. His reign is full of Elisha stories: the Moab campaign, Naaman, and the siege of Samaria. Jehu killed him at Jezreel, ending Omri's dynasty.
textSays: Reigned twelve years; did evil but removed the pillar of Baal (2 Kgs 3:1-3). Campaign against Moab (2 Kgs 3:6-27). Probably the unnamed 'king of Israel' in several Elisha stories (2 Kgs 5-7). Killed by Jehu (2 Kgs 9:24). The synchronisms of 2 Kgs 1:17 and 2 Kgs 3:1 differ, which Thiele explains by a co-regency in Judah (debated).
voice: Erratic and defensive; swings between panic, blame and grudging respect for the prophet.

events.title: Kills his brothers
events.summary: Once secure on the throne he kills all six brothers and some officials.

events.title: Edom and Libnah revolt
events.summary: Edom throws off Judah's rule and sets up its own king; Libnah also revolts.

events.title: Letter from Elijah
events.summary: A letter from Elijah condemns him for following Ahab's house and killing his better brothers and warns of a disease of the bowels.

events.title: Death without honour
events.summary: Philistines and Arabians plunder his house and take his sons except the youngest. He dies in agony and 'departed with no one's regret'.

summary: Jehoram, son of Jehoshaphat, reigned over Judah for eight years, probably as co-regent with his father from about 853 BC and alone from about 848 to 841 BC. He married Athaliah, daughter of Ahab, and the verdict of the text is that he 'walked in the way of the kings of Israel, as the house of Ahab had done'. He murdered his brothers, lost Edom, and died of a painful disease unmourned. Yet the LORD would not destroy David's house, because of his covenant promise.
textSays: Reigned eight years; married Ahab's daughter and did evil (2 Kgs 8:16-18). The LORD spared Judah for David's sake (2 Kgs 8:19). Edom revolted (2 Kgs 8:20-22). Killed his brothers (2 Chr 21:4). Elijah's letter (2 Chr 21:12-15). Died unmourned, not buried in the kings' tombs (2 Chr 21:19-20). In Jesus' genealogy as Joram (Matt 1:8).

interpretations.view: 2 Kings 3 suggests Elijah had been taken up before this time, so some say the letter was written in advance, some that Elijah's departure is narrated out of chronological order, and others that Chronicles is using a later tradition (debated).

voice: Suspicious and ruthless; a man who secures power by removing rivals.

events.title: Follows his mother's counsel
events.summary: His mother Athaliah and the house of Ahab advise him to do wickedly, 'to his undoing'.

events.title: Joins Joram against Hazael
events.summary: He fights alongside his uncle Joram of Israel at Ramoth-gilead and then visits the wounded Joram at Jezreel.

events.title: Killed in Jehu's purge
events.summary: Caught up in Jehu's revolt, he flees, is wounded near Ibleam and dies at Megiddo. He is buried in Jerusalem for Jehoshaphat's sake.

summary: Ahaziah, son of Jehoram and Athaliah, reigned over Judah for one year (841 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, following the house of Ahab, to which he was related by marriage. Visiting his wounded uncle at Jezreel, he was swept up in Jehu's revolt and killed. His death opened the way for his mother Athaliah to seize power and try to wipe out the royal family.
textSays: Twenty-two when he began to reign, reigned one year; his mother was Athaliah (2 Kgs 8:26). Did evil like the house of Ahab (2 Kgs 8:27). Killed by Jehu's men (2 Kgs 9:27). 2 Chr 22:2 in the Hebrew says forty-two, which would make him older than his father; most versions follow 2 Kgs 8:26 and some Greek and Syriac witnesses with twenty-two (scholarly-consensus that forty-two is a copying error).
voice: Young, easily led and eager to belong to his powerful relatives in the north.

events.title: Hides a hundred prophets
events.summary: While Jezebel is killing the LORD's prophets, he hides a hundred of them in two caves and feeds them bread and water.

events.title: Meets Elijah during the drought
events.summary: Sent by Ahab to search for grass, he meets Elijah, who tells him to announce him to Ahab. Afraid Elijah will vanish and Ahab will kill him, he hesitates, but Elijah swears to appear, and Obadiah carries the message.

summary: Obadiah was the official in charge of King Ahab's palace and a man who 'feared the LORD greatly'. Working inside Ahab's government, he secretly saved a hundred prophets from Jezebel's purge. During the drought he became the reluctant go-between who arranged the meeting of Elijah and Ahab that led to the contest on Mount Carmel. He is generally distinguished from the prophet Obadiah who wrote the book.
textSays: Over Ahab's household; feared the LORD greatly (1 Kgs 18:3). Hid and fed a hundred prophets (1 Kgs 18:4). Feared the LORD from his youth (1 Kgs 18:12). Arranged the meeting of Elijah and Ahab (1 Kgs 18:16).

interpretations.view: The Talmud (Sanhedrin 39b) identifies him with the prophet Obadiah, an Edomite convert, and later Jewish lore names him as husband of the widow helped by Elisha in 2 Kings 4 (tradition).

Often discussed as a model, or a test case, of serving faithfully inside a corrupt government. Most scholars date the book of Obadiah much later and do not identify him with its author (scholarly-consensus).

voice: Careful, devout and anxious; a loyal insider who weighs every risk and still does the right thing.

events.title: Builds a room for Elisha
events.summary: A wealthy woman of Shunem, she persuades Elisha to eat with her and has a small upper room furnished for him.

events.title: Promised a son
events.summary: She asks nothing for herself, but Gehazi notes she has no son and her husband is old. Elisha promises a son, and she bears one the next year.

events.title: Son dies and is raised
events.summary: The boy dies in her arms. She lays him on Elisha's bed, rides to Mount Carmel, clings to Elisha's feet and will not leave without him. Elisha prays, stretches himself on the child, and he lives.

events.title: Land restored
events.summary: Warned of a seven-year famine, she lives among the Philistines. Returning to claim her land, she arrives just as Gehazi is telling the king her story, and the king restores everything.

summary: The woman of Shunem, a town in the Jezreel Valley, was a wealthy and generous Israelite who gave Elisha a room to stay in on his travels. She asked for nothing, but Elisha promised her a son. When the boy died, she went straight to Elisha with fierce determination, and he raised him to life. Years later the king restored her land after hearing her story. She is one of the most strong-willed and admirable figures in the Elisha stories.
textSays: A 'great woman' of Shunem who provided for Elisha (2 Kgs 4:8-10). Promised and given a son (2 Kgs 4:16-17). Son raised (2 Kgs 4:32-37). Moved to Philistia during famine and had her land restored (2 Kgs 8:1-6). Hebrews may allude to her among 'women who received back their dead' (Heb 11:35).

interpretations.view: Her story, with the widow of Zarephath's, is seen as a foreshadowing of resurrection; Jesus' raising of the son of the widow of Nain at nearby Nain is often compared.

voice: Composed, self-reliant and direct; says 'it is well' through her grief and refuses to let go until help comes.

events.title: Serves the Shunammite
events.summary: He relays Elisha's messages and points out that the woman has no son.

events.title: Fails to raise the boy
events.summary: Sent ahead with Elisha's staff to lay on the dead child, he reports, 'The child has not awakened.'

events.title: Greed and leprosy
events.summary: After Elisha refuses Naaman's gifts, Gehazi runs after him, lies that Elisha wants silver and clothes, and hides them. Elisha confronts him, and Naaman's leprosy clings to Gehazi and his descendants.

events.title: Tells the king of Elisha's deeds
events.summary: Later he recounts Elisha's miracles to the king, just as the Shunammite arrives.

summary: Gehazi was the servant of the prophet Elisha. He was practical and observant, but when Elisha refused payment from the Aramean general Naaman, Gehazi secretly ran after him and lied to get silver and clothing. Elisha exposed him, and Naaman's skin disease came upon him. He appears once more, telling the king about Elisha's great deeds. His story contrasts a foreign general who learns grace with an Israelite insider who turns it into profit.
textSays: Elisha's servant (2 Kgs 4:12). Could not wake the boy with the staff (2 Kgs 4:31). Took gifts from Naaman by deception (2 Kgs 5:20-24). Struck with leprosy 'white as snow' (2 Kgs 5:27). Later told the king Elisha's deeds (2 Kgs 8:4-5).

interpretations.view: Rabbinic lists name him among commoners who lost their share in the world to come (Mishnah Sanhedrin 10:2), and later stories cast him as a sceptic; this is tradition, not text.

Often paired with Judas and with Ananias and Sapphira as a warning against greed in ministry. Some suggest 2 Kgs 8 shows him partly restored, since he speaks with the king; others take the stories as out of order (debated).

voice: Quick, practical and a little calculating; talks fast when he thinks no one is watching.

events.title: Feeds Elijah with her last meal
events.summary: Gathering sticks to cook a final meal for herself and her son, she is asked by Elijah to make him a cake first. She trusts his promise, and her jar of flour and jug of oil do not run out through the drought.

events.title: Son raised to life
events.summary: Her son dies and she blames Elijah. He carries the boy upstairs, cries to the LORD and stretches himself on him three times. The boy lives, and she says, 'Now I know that you are a man of God.'

events.title: Cited by Jesus
events.summary: In Nazareth Jesus points out that among many widows in Israel, Elijah was sent only to this foreign widow.

summary: The widow of Zarephath lived in a Phoenician town near Sidon, Jezebel's homeland, during the great drought. Down to her last handful of flour, she fed Elijah first on the strength of God's promise, and her supplies lasted until the rain. When her son died, Elijah raised him, the first resurrection recorded in the Bible. Jesus later used her to show that God's mercy reached outsiders, which enraged his hometown.
textSays: A widow at Zarephath of Sidon commanded to feed Elijah (1 Kgs 17:9). Flour and oil did not fail (1 Kgs 17:16). Her son died and was revived (1 Kgs 17:17-22). She confessed Elijah as a man of God whose word is truth (1 Kgs 17:24). Jesus cites her (Luke 4:25-26).

interpretations.view: Some midrashic traditions identify her son with the prophet Jonah (tradition).
Seen as an example of Gentile faith and of God's care for the poor and foreign, and as a foreshadowing of resurrection.

voice: Honest and worn down by hardship, plain about her poverty and her grief; slowly moving from desperation to faith.

events.title: Named in Elijah's commission
events.summary: At Horeb God tells Elijah to anoint Hazael king over Aram as an instrument of judgment.

events.title: Elisha weeps over him
events.summary: Sent by the sick Ben-hadad to consult Elisha, he is told he will be king and will do terrible harm to Israel. Elisha stares at him and weeps.

events.title: Seizes the throne
events.summary: The next day he smothers Ben-hadad with a wet cloth and becomes king.

events.title: Cuts Israel down
events.summary: He takes all Israel's land east of the Jordan and oppresses Israel through Jehu's and Jehoahaz's reigns.

events.title: Threatens Jerusalem
events.summary: He captures Gath and turns toward Jerusalem; Joash of Judah buys him off with the temple treasures.

summary: Hazael was an official of Ben-hadad who murdered his master and became king of Aram-Damascus in about 842 BC. Elisha wept when he foresaw the cruelty Hazael would inflict on Israel. As king he took all of Israel's territory east of the Jordan, pressed deep into Philistia and forced Judah to pay him off. Assyrian records call him 'son of a nobody', meaning a usurper, and he is widely thought to be the author of the Tel Dan inscription, which mentions the 'house of David'.
textSays: To be anointed by Elijah (1 Kgs 19:15). Elisha foretold his kingship and cruelty (2 Kgs 8:12-13). Killed Ben-hadad (2 Kgs 8:15). Fought Joram at Ramoth-gilead (2 Kgs 8:28). Reduced Israel (2 Kgs 10:32). Took Gath; Joash paid tribute (2 Kgs 12:17-18). His son Ben-hadad lost cities to Israel (2 Kgs 13:24-25). Amos announces fire on 'the house of Hazael' (Amos 1:4).

interpretations.view: Shalmaneser III's inscriptions call Hazael a 'son of nobody' who seized the throne (scholarly-consensus). Most scholars attribute the Tel Dan Stele, which claims victory over a king of Israel and a king of the 'house of David', to Hazael, though some debate the authorship and reading (debated).
The text records no anointing by Elijah; Elisha's encounter is usually read as fulfilling Elijah's commission through his successor.

voice: Smooth and deferential in front of the prophet, ruthless in private; speaks with false modesty ('what is your servant, a dog?').

roles: royal name of several kings of Aram-Damascus

events.title: Bribed by Asa against Baasha
events.summary: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon takes Asa's gold, breaks his treaty with Baasha and conquers towns in northern Israel.

events.title: Besieges Samaria and loses
events.summary: Ben-hadad, with thirty-two allied kings, demands Ahab's wealth and family. While drinking in his tent, his army is routed.

events.title: Defeated at Aphek and spared
events.summary: Claiming Israel's god rules only the hills, he fights in the plain and loses again. Ahab spares him on generous terms, and a prophet condemns Ahab for it.

events.title: Wars with Elisha's Israel
events.summary: His raids are foiled by Elisha's warnings; an army sent to seize Elisha at Dothan is struck blind. His siege of Samaria ends when his army flees at a noise from the LORD.

events.title: Killed by Hazael
events.summary: Sick, he sends Hazael to ask Elisha if he will recover; Hazael smothers him and takes the throne.

summary: Ben-hadad, 'son of Hadad' (the Aramean storm god), was a name or title used by several kings of Damascus, Israel's main rival to the north in the ninth and eighth centuries BC. The Bible mentions at least two and probably three: Ben-hadad son of Tabrimmon, whom Asa hired against Baasha; the Ben-hadad who fought Ahab and Joram and was murdered by Hazael; and Hazael's son Ben-hadad, who lost cities back to Israel. Scholars debate whether the first two are the same man and how the second relates to the 'Hadadezer' of Assyrian records.
textSays: Son of Tabrimmon, son of Hezion (1 Kgs 15:18). Fought Ahab at Samaria and Aphek (1 Kgs 20:1-34). Besieged Samaria in Elisha's day (2 Kgs 6:24). Killed by Hazael (2 Kgs 8:15). Ben-hadad son of Hazael defeated three times by Jehoash of Israel (2 Kgs 13:24-25). The 'strongholds of Ben-hadad' will burn (Jer 49:27; Amos 1:4).

interpretations.view: Some count Ben-hadad I (Asa's time), Ben-hadad II (Ahab's foe) and Ben-hadad III (Hazael's son); others think Ben-hadad I and II were one long-reigning king. Assyrian records name Hadadezer as Damascus' king at the battle of Qarqar in 853 BC, leading some to think 'Ben-hadad' in 1 Kgs 20 is a title or that the stories have been rearranged (debated).
The Melqart Stele mentions a 'Bar-Hadad', and the Zakkur inscription names Bar-Hadad son of Hazael (scholarly-consensus on Zakkur; the Melqart reading is debated).

voice: Boastful and theatrical in strength, wheedling in defeat; fond of grand demands and drinking-tent bravado.

events.title: Hides the infant Joash
events.summary: When Athaliah kills the royal family, his wife Jehosheba rescues baby Joash, and they hide him in the temple for six years.

events.title: Crowns Joash and topples Athaliah
events.summary: He organises the guards and Levites, crowns the seven-year-old Joash in the temple, and has Athaliah executed outside the temple grounds.

events.title: Covenant renewal
events.summary: He makes a covenant between the LORD, king and people; the people tear down Baal's temple and kill its priest Mattan.

events.title: Guides Joash's reign
events.summary: Joash does right all the days Jehoiada instructs him, including repairing the temple with a collection chest.

events.title: Buried among the kings
events.summary: He dies at 130 and is buried with the kings because he had done good in Israel.

summary: Jehoiada was the chief priest in Jerusalem who saved David's royal line. When Queen Athaliah murdered the heirs to the throne, he and his wife Jehosheba hid the infant Joash in the temple for six years, then staged a carefully planned coup, crowned the boy and had Athaliah executed. He led a covenant renewal, cleared out Baal worship and guided Joash for decades. After his death Joash turned away and even had Jehoiada's son Zechariah stoned.
textSays: Organised the coronation of Joash (2 Kgs 11:4-12). Ordered Athaliah's death (2 Kgs 11:15). Made a covenant (2 Kgs 11:17). Joash did right all his days because Jehoiada instructed him (2 Kgs 12:2). Married Jehosheba, daughter of King Jehoram (2 Chr 22:11). Died at 130, buried with kings (2 Chr 24:15-16). After his death Joash turned to idols and killed his son Zechariah (2 Chr 24:17-22). Not the father of Benaiah, who belongs to David's time.

interpretations.view: Many link Jesus' words about the blood of Zechariah 'between the sanctuary and the altar' (Luke 11:51) to Jehoiada's son, since Chronicles ends the Hebrew Bible; Matthew's 'son of Barachiah' complicates this (debated).

voice: Authoritative, patient and strategic; a priest who speaks of covenant and acts with a soldier's planning.

events.title: Restores Israel's borders
events.summary: He wins back territory from Lebo-hamath to the Dead Sea, as the prophet Jonah son of Amittai had foretold, because the LORD saw Israel's bitter suffering.

events.title: Amos denounces his kingdom
events.summary: Amos prophesies that God will rise against the house of Jeroboam with the sword. The priest Amaziah of Bethel reports this to the king and tells Amos to go home to Judah.

summary: Jeroboam II, son of Joash and great-grandson of Jehu, reigned over Israel for forty-one years (about 793 to 753 BC, including a co-regency with his father). The verdict of the text is that he did evil, keeping the sins of Jeroboam I. Yet God used him to restore Israel's borders, and his reign was the northern kingdom's last era of wealth and power. The prophets Amos and Hosea show the dark side of that prosperity: luxury for the rich, injustice for the poor and empty religion. Within thirty years of his death the kingdom had fallen to Assyria.
textSays: Reigned forty-one years in Samaria and did evil (2 Kgs 14:23-24). Restored Israel's border as Jonah prophesied (2 Kgs 14:25). God saved Israel by him because he had not said he would blot out Israel's name (2 Kgs 14:26-27). Recovered Damascus and Hamath (2 Kgs 14:28). Named in the headings of Hosea and Amos (Hos 1:1; Amos 1:1). His son Zechariah reigned six months (2 Kgs 15:8-12).

interpretations.view: A seal from Megiddo inscribed 'Shema servant of Jeroboam' is usually linked to Jeroboam II, and the Samaria ostraca are often dated to his reign (scholarly-consensus on the seal's date range; attribution debated).

voice: Self-assured and prosperous; speaks like a successful king who sees no need for prophets' warnings.

events.title: Kills Shallum and takes the throne
events.summary: Coming up from Tirzah, he kills Shallum, who had reigned only a month after assassinating Zechariah.

events.title: Atrocity at Tiphsah
events.summary: When Tiphsah refuses to open its gates, he sacks it and rips open its pregnant women.

events.title: Pays tribute to Pul
events.summary: When Pul (Tiglath-pileser III) of Assyria invades, Menahem pays a thousand talents of silver, raised by taxing every wealthy man fifty shekels, to keep his throne.

summary: Menahem seized Israel's throne in a coup and reigned about ten years (around 752 to 742 BC). The verdict of the text is that he did evil all his days. He was notoriously brutal, and he kept power by paying a huge tribute to the Assyrian king Tiglath-pileser III (called Pul). Assyrian annals list 'Menihimmu of Samaria' among their tribute-payers, one of several points where the Bible and Assyrian records match. His son Pekahiah was murdered by Pekah after two years.
textSays: Son of Gadi; killed Shallum (2 Kgs 15:14). Sacked Tiphsah with atrocities (2 Kgs 15:16). Reigned ten years and did evil (2 Kgs 15:17-18). Paid Pul a thousand talents (2 Kgs 15:19-20). Succeeded by his son Pekahiah (2 Kgs 15:22).

interpretations.view: Tiglath-pileser III's annals record tribute from Menahem, usually dated about 740-738 BC; this creates tension with Thiele's end date of 742 and is one reason chronologies differ (debated).

voice: Brutal, transactional and wary; speaks of silver and survival.

alternatives.label: Short reign view (Albright and others, 20 years read as a later total)

events.title: Assassinates Pekahiah
events.summary: As an officer, with fifty men of Gilead, he kills King Pekahiah in the citadel of Samaria.

events.title: Allies with Rezin against Judah
events.summary: With Rezin of Damascus he attacks Jerusalem to force Ahaz into an anti-Assyrian alliance. Isaiah tells Ahaz not to fear these 'two smouldering stumps of firebrands'.

events.title: Massive victory over Judah
events.summary: He kills 120,000 Judeans in a day; the prophet Oded persuades the army to free the captives.

events.title: Loses Galilee and his life
events.summary: Tiglath-pileser III takes Gilead, Galilee and Naphtali and deports the people. Hoshea son of Elah assassinates Pekah.

summary: Pekah, son of Remaliah, was an army officer who killed King Pekahiah and took Israel's throne. The text gives him twenty years, which Thiele explains by a rival reign in Gilead from about 752 BC before he ruled in Samaria from about 740 to 732 BC; others think the number is a later miscalculation. The verdict of the text is that he did evil. He joined Rezin of Damascus against Assyria and attacked Judah, prompting Isaiah's famous Immanuel prophecy. Assyria responded by stripping Israel of Galilee and Gilead, and Pekah was murdered by Hoshea.
textSays: Killed Pekahiah (2 Kgs 15:25). Reigned twenty years and did evil (2 Kgs 15:27-28). Lost territory to Tiglath-pileser (2 Kgs 15:29). Killed by Hoshea (2 Kgs 15:30). Attacked Jerusalem with Rezin (2 Kgs 16:5; Isa 7:1). Isaiah dismisses him as 'the son of Remaliah' (Isa 7:4-9).

interpretations.view: Thiele and many followers posit an overlapping rival reign; others (for example Albright, Galil) shorten his reign and treat the twenty years as a later editorial figure (debated).
Tiglath-pileser III claims that Israel overthrew 'Paqaha' and that he installed 'Ausi' (Hoshea) as king (scholarly-consensus).

voice: Bold, hard-edged and anti-Assyrian; a soldier-politician gambling on alliances.

events.title: Kills Pekah and becomes king
events.summary: He conspires against Pekah and kills him.

events.title: Vassal of Assyria
events.summary: Shalmaneser V comes against him and he becomes a tribute-paying vassal.

events.title: Seeks Egypt's help and is imprisoned
events.summary: He sends envoys to 'So, king of Egypt' and stops paying tribute. Shalmaneser arrests and imprisons him.

events.title: Fall of Samaria
events.summary: After a three-year siege Samaria falls in Hoshea's ninth year, and the Assyrians deport Israel. The northern kingdom ends.

summary: Hoshea, son of Elah, was the last king of the northern kingdom of Israel, reigning about nine years (around 732 to 723/722 BC). He killed Pekah and ruled as an Assyrian vassal, then gambled on help from Egypt and stopped paying tribute. Assyria imprisoned him, besieged Samaria for three years and deported its people. The verdict of the text is that he did evil, 'yet not as the kings of Israel who were before him'. 2 Kings 17 follows his reign with a long sermon on why Israel fell.
textSays: Killed Pekah (2 Kgs 15:30). Reigned nine years; did evil, but not like his predecessors (2 Kgs 17:1-2). Became Shalmaneser's vassal, then conspired with So of Egypt and was imprisoned (2 Kgs 17:3-4). Samaria taken in his ninth year (2 Kgs 17:6). Israel fell because they sinned against the LORD (2 Kgs 17:7-23).

interpretations.view: Tiglath-pileser III claims to have placed Hoshea on the throne. 'So' is variously identified with Osorkon IV, with Tefnakht, or read as the city of Sais (debated). Both Shalmaneser V and Sargon II claimed the capture of Samaria (debated).
The Talmud suggests Hoshea was judged less harshly because he removed guards that Jeroboam had set to stop pilgrims going to Jerusalem (tradition).

voice: Anxious and calculating, a vassal king playing great powers against each other with too few cards.

alternatives.label: Earlier end to match Hezekiah's accession in 2 Kgs 18:1

events.title: Sacrifices his son
events.summary: He makes his son 'pass through the fire', following the abhorrent practices of the nations.

events.title: Refuses Isaiah's sign
events.summary: Threatened by Rezin and Pekah, he is told by Isaiah to stand firm in faith and to ask for a sign. He piously refuses, and Isaiah gives the sign of Immanuel anyway.

events.title: Becomes Assyria's vassal
events.summary: He sends temple and palace silver and gold to Tiglath-pileser: 'I am your servant and your son.' Assyria takes Damascus and kills Rezin.

events.title: Copies the Damascus altar
events.summary: Visiting Tiglath-pileser in Damascus, he sends a model of an altar to the priest Uriah, installs it in the temple and moves the bronze altar aside.

events.title: Shuts the temple doors
events.summary: Under pressure, he sacrifices to the gods of Damascus, cuts up the temple vessels and closes the doors of the LORD's house.

summary: Ahaz, son of Jotham, reigned over Judah for sixteen years, roughly 735 to 715 BC (the exact dates are debated because of overlapping reigns). The verdict of the text is that he 'did not do what was right in the eyes of the LORD' and was one of Judah's worst kings: he sacrificed his son in fire and brought foreign worship into the temple. When Israel and Aram attacked him, Isaiah urged him to trust God, but he turned to Assyria and became its vassal. Isaiah's Immanuel prophecy was first spoken to him. His son Hezekiah reversed his policies.
textSays: Reigned sixteen years; did not do right, burned his son as an offering (2 Kgs 16:2-4). Attacked by Rezin and Pekah (2 Kgs 16:5). Paid Tiglath-pileser for help (2 Kgs 16:7-8). Built a copy of the Damascus altar (2 Kgs 16:10-16). Shut the temple doors (2 Chr 28:24). Isaiah's encounter and the Immanuel sign (Isa 7:1-17). The 'dial of Ahaz' (2 Kgs 20:11; Isa 38:8). In Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:9).

interpretations.view: Jewish interpreters and many modern scholars see the sign as first fulfilled in a child born in Ahaz's time (perhaps Hezekiah or Isaiah's son). Matthew applies it to Jesus' virgin birth (Matt 1:22-23); Christians variously see direct prediction, double fulfilment, or typological fulfilment (debated).
