A clay bulla reads 'Belonging to Ahaz son of Jotham, king of Judah', and Tiglath-pileser III lists 'Jehoahaz of Judah' among tribute-payers (scholarly-consensus).

voice: Politically clever and spiritually evasive; uses pious words ('I will not test the LORD') to avoid trusting him.

events.title: Executes his father's killers, spares their sons
events.summary: He executes the servants who assassinated Joash but not their children, obeying the law that each person dies for his own sin (Deut 24:16).

events.title: Victory over Edom; worships its gods
events.summary: He kills ten thousand Edomites in the Valley of Salt, then brings home Edom's gods and worships them, rejecting a prophet's rebuke.

events.title: Challenges Jehoash of Israel
events.summary: Proud after Edom, he challenges Israel. Jehoash replies with a fable of a thistle and a cedar, then defeats him at Beth-shemesh, breaks down Jerusalem's wall and loots the temple.

events.title: Killed at Lachish
events.summary: A conspiracy forms in Jerusalem; he flees to Lachish and is killed there.

summary: Amaziah, son of Joash, reigned over Judah for twenty-nine years (about 796 to 767 BC, overlapping with his son Uzziah's co-regency). The verdict of the text is that he did what was right, 'yet not like David', and Chronicles adds 'not with a whole heart'. He began justly and defeated Edom, but then worshipped Edom's captured gods and foolishly provoked Israel, which humiliated him and plundered Jerusalem. Like his father, he died by assassination.
textSays: Reigned twenty-nine years; did right but not like David; high places remained (2 Kgs 14:1-4). Spared the killers' children (2 Kgs 14:6). Defeated Edom (2 Kgs 14:7). Defeated by Jehoash (2 Kgs 14:11-14). Killed at Lachish (2 Kgs 14:19). Chronicles: hired and then dismissed Israelite mercenaries (2 Chr 25:6-10), worshipped Edom's gods (2 Chr 25:14), rejected the prophet (2 Chr 25:15-16).
voice: Ambitious and touchy; quick to take credit, slow to take advice.

alternatives.label: Thiele, end of his effective rule; lived to about 732

events.title: Governs for Uzziah
events.summary: When his father Uzziah is struck with leprosy, Jotham governs the palace and judges the people.

events.title: Builds the Upper Gate and forts
events.summary: He builds the upper gate of the temple, works on the wall of Ophel, and builds cities and towers in Judah's hills and forests.

events.title: Subdues Ammon
events.summary: He defeats the Ammonites and receives tribute for three years.

summary: Jotham, son of Uzziah, ruled Judah as regent while his father was a leper and then as king, about 750 to 735 BC by Thiele's reckoning (the overlap with Ahaz is debated). The verdict of the text is that he did what was right, as his father had, though the people still acted corruptly and the high places remained. Chronicles says he 'became mighty because he ordered his ways before the LORD'. He was a builder and successful in war. Isaiah, Hosea and Micah were active in his days.
textSays: Governed for Uzziah (2 Kgs 15:5). Reigned sixteen years; did right like Uzziah; high places remained (2 Kgs 15:32-35). Did not enter the temple as his father had (2 Chr 27:2). Became mighty because he ordered his ways before the LORD (2 Chr 27:6). Named in Isa 1:1, Hos 1:1 and Mic 1:1, and in Jesus' genealogy (Matt 1:9).

interpretations.view: 2 Kgs 15:30 mentions a 'twentieth year of Jotham', more than his sixteen-year reign. Thiele explains this by counting from the start of his co-regency and supposing Ahaz took effective control while Jotham was still alive; others suspect a scribal or editorial issue (debated).

voice: Steady, quiet and methodical; a builder who prefers careful work to grand speeches.

events.title: Pays tribute to Israel
events.summary: As a sheep breeder-king he pays Israel a heavy tribute in lambs and wool.

events.title: Rebels after Ahab dies
events.summary: When Ahab dies he refuses to pay.

events.title: Sacrifices his son on the wall
events.summary: Beaten back and besieged at Kir-hareseth by Israel, Judah and Edom, he offers his eldest son as a burnt offering on the city wall. 'Great wrath' comes upon Israel and the allies withdraw.

summary: Mesha was king of Moab, east of the Dead Sea, in the ninth century BC. He paid Israel heavy tribute in sheep and wool until Ahab died, then rebelled. When a coalition of Israel, Judah and Edom besieged him, he sacrificed his heir on the city wall, and the attackers withdrew. Mesha's own account survives on the Mesha Stele (Moabite Stone, about 840 BC), which credits his god Chemosh with freeing Moab from Omri's house and mentions Israel and very probably the LORD (YHWH) by name.
textSays: A sheep breeder who paid Israel 100,000 lambs and the wool of 100,000 rams (2 Kgs 3:4). Rebelled after Ahab's death (2 Kgs 3:5). Sacrificed his eldest son; great wrath came on Israel and they withdrew (2 Kgs 3:27).

interpretations.view: Readers differ on whose wrath this is: God's anger at Israel, the fury of Moab spurred by the sacrifice, the allies' horror, or (in some critical readings) the power of Chemosh as the original story imagined it (debated).

The Mesha Stele, found in 1868, confirms Mesha, Omri, and Israel's domination of Moab; its account of how and when Moab broke free differs from 2 Kings 3 in emphasis and perhaps timing (scholarly-consensus on the stele's authenticity; details debated).

voice: Proud and pious toward his own god; boasts in the style of an ancient victory inscription.
